headline_en: Call for coordinated action to stop technology-driven human trafficking
summary_en: Video page for a Prothom Alo roundtable titled 'Fraud and human trafficking in the trap of technology: what is to be done?'. The short text says online fraud and the risk of human trafficking are rising along with technological progress. The page gives no speakers, figures or recommendations; the content is in the video.

facts.statement: Prothom Alo held a roundtable at its office titled 'Prothukti-r fande protarona o manab pachar: koronio ki?' (Fraud and human trafficking in the trap of technology: what is to be done?); the text page carries no details of what was said, which is only in the video.
Prothom Alo's video page (published 30 July 2026) states that online fraud and the risk of human trafficking are increasing in step with technological advances.

headline_en: Kuwait: one app with hundreds of services has changed citizen services; where is Bangladesh
summary_en: An opinion piece by the president of the Bangladesh Press Club in Kuwait describes Kuwait's 'Sahel' government app, through which citizens and expatriates handle residency (iqama) checks, health insurance status, work permit information, traffic fines, government notices and fee payments from a phone. It gives the app's launch date, growth in services and users, and contrasts it with Bangladesh's fragmented digital services, urging a single app in Bangladesh.

facts.statement: Kuwait's government runs an integrated digital platform called 'Sahel' (Arabic for easy/simple) through which citizens and expatriates can use more than a hundred government services from a mobile phone, instead of going from office to office.
facts.source_in_article: Moin Uddin Sarkar Sumon, president, Bangladesh Press Club Kuwait (opinion piece)

facts.statement: Through the Sahel app, expatriates in Kuwait can check the validity of their residency or iqama, check health insurance status, see work permit (labour permit) information, receive government notices and pay various fees, each within a few minutes, according to the writer.
facts.source_in_article: Moin Uddin Sarkar Sumon, president, Bangladesh Press Club Kuwait (opinion piece)

facts.statement: Sahel app users in Kuwait can also handle their identity card, residence-related information, traffic fines, health services, court notices, labour permits and government fee payments from home; applicants can track the whole process of application, approval and notification on the phone.
facts.source_in_article: Moin Uddin Sarkar Sumon, president, Bangladesh Press Club Kuwait (opinion piece)

facts.statement: Kuwait's citizen-and-expatriate government services app is named 'Sahel' (সাহেল).
facts.source_in_article: Moin Uddin Sarkar Sumon, president, Bangladesh Press Club Kuwait (opinion piece)

facts.statement: According to the Kuwait government (as cited by the writer), the Sahel app was formally launched in September 2021 and began operating for citizens and expatriates from 15 September 2021, starting with only 123 government services and 14 government bodies.
facts.source_in_article: Moin Uddin Sarkar Sumon, president, Bangladesh Press Club Kuwait (opinion piece)

facts.statement: The Sahel app now covers more than 450 services and several dozen government institutions on one platform, according to the writer.
facts.source_in_article: Moin Uddin Sarkar Sumon, president, Bangladesh Press Club Kuwait (opinion piece)

facts.statement: By 2025, more than 111 million digital transactions had been completed through Kuwait's Sahel app and the number of users had passed about 2.9 million, according to the writer.
facts.source_in_article: Moin Uddin Sarkar Sumon, president, Bangladesh Press Club Kuwait (opinion piece)

facts.statement: About 2.5 to 3 million expatriates live in Kuwait, according to the writer.
facts.source_in_article: Moin Uddin Sarkar Sumon, president, Bangladesh Press Club Kuwait (opinion piece)

facts.statement: Sahel was launched as part of Kuwait's 'New Kuwait 2035' digital transformation programme, aiming to reduce trips to government offices by citizens and expatriates.
facts.source_in_article: Moin Uddin Sarkar Sumon, president, Bangladesh Press Club Kuwait (opinion piece)

facts.statement: The writer says the Sahel app has reduced expatriates' dependence on brokers (middlemen) in Kuwait, reduced crowds in government offices and cut opportunities for bribery and harassment.
facts.source_in_article: Moin Uddin Sarkar Sumon, president, Bangladesh Press Club Kuwait (opinion piece)

facts.statement: The writer says Bangladesh services such as e-passport, e-mutation (e-namjari), online land development tax and the national information portal are digital, but systems are separate (land, passport, tax, courts and police each on different platforms), applicants often still must go to offices to submit papers, ministries' data are not linked, and middlemen and brokers' influence has not been removed.
facts.source_in_article: Moin Uddin Sarkar Sumon, president, Bangladesh Press Club Kuwait (opinion piece)

facts.statement: Readers can send stories, news, videos and photos about life abroad to Prothom Alo's 'Dur Porobash' section by email at dp@prothomalo.com.

headline_en: Found through a Facebook video, Isak Mia returns to relatives after 45 years
summary_en: Isak Mia, nearly 70, from Lakshmipur village, Burishwar union, Nasirnagar upazila, Brahmanbaria, sold family land for 75,000 taka in the 1980s hoping to go abroad (to London, per his nephew), went to Sylhet and was cheated by a broker. He never went abroad or returned home, and spent about 45 years wandering, now mentally unwell. After a media Facebook video showed him at Kumarkhali railway station in Kushtia, relatives came and the upazila administration handed him over to them on a Tuesday (about 2 June 2026).

facts.statement: In the 1980s Isak Mia of Nasirnagar, Brahmanbaria, sold two bighas of farmland and 40 decimals of homestead land for 75,000 taka to go abroad, went to Sylhet, and fell into the trap of a broker (dalal) who took the money; he never went abroad.
facts.source_in_article: Isak Mia; nephew Bachchu Mia; Kumarkhali upazila administration and relatives

facts.statement: Isak Mia's family (seven siblings together, per nephew Bachchu Mia) sold two bighas of farmland and a homestead including 40 decimals of land for 75,000 taka about 45 years ago so that Isak could go to London; Isak said a broker in Sylhet took the money.

After losing the money to a broker, Isak Mia did not return home and spent about 45 years in streets, markets and stations; he is now described as mentally unbalanced and unable to function, aged nearly 70.

Isak Mia was traced after a media outlet's Facebook page posted a video of him at Kumarkhali railway station (Kushtia); relatives contacted local journalist Monowar and came to Kumarkhali; after verification the Kumarkhali upazila administration handed him over to two nephews and relatives on Tuesday afternoon.
facts.source_in_article: UNO Farzana Akhter; nephew Sajahan Mia

facts.statement: Local businessman Abu Bakkar Siddique said Isak Mia was found unconscious beside Kumarkhali station 26 days earlier; locals arranged treatment and food before news reports led relatives to him.
